## How this sheet works

Exercises rederive or apply the lecture's results. Do them on your own
time; they are not worked in class. The class works the discussions,
the problems and the coding under "In class," in that order.
Discussions are in groups of three or four, then with the room. Each
problem, and the coding, is gone through as soon as the room has tried
it.

Every item is about one decision: who is in the data, what is recorded
about them, and what to do about the people and the columns that are
not there. Someone made that decision, usually not the people left
out, and every way of handling what is missing is an assumption about
people nobody asked. So each item ends by asking who the mistake falls
on, who gains from it going unnoticed, or who the choice could be
justified to. The arithmetic is how you earn an answer to that
question; it is not the answer.

Notation as in the lecture: $C = 1$ if a person's $Y$ is recorded and
$C = 0$ if it is missing; $e(X) = P(C = 1 \mid X)$; $A$ is a group.

## Exercises

Attempt each part before you open a hint.

::: {.callout-warning title="Hints"}
Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few
minutes, and open them in order.
:::

### Exercise 1. Selection on a collider, by hand

A company's records cover the people it hired. It hired every applicant
who either did well at the interview or had a referral from a current
employee. Among applicants, half did well at the interview and half had
a referral, independently of each other.

(a) Among the people hired, what fraction of those with a referral did
well at the interview? What fraction of those without a referral?

(b) Draw the causal graph with three nodes: interview, referral, hired.
Which node do the company's records condition on?

(c) The company notices that referred hires did worse at interview than
other hires, concludes that referrals attract weaker candidates, and
raises the interview bar for referred applicants. What is wrong with
the conclusion, and who pays for it?

(d) Redo (a) when a fraction $q$ of applicants do well at the interview,
whatever $q$ is. Does the gap between the two fractions depend on $q$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
Start with the hires who have no referral. How did each of them get in?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
Among the applicants with a referral, the hiring rule kept everyone.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) Everyone without a referral was hired only because they did well at
the interview, so that fraction is $1$. Those with a referral were hired
whatever their interview, so among them the interview fraction is the
applicants' fraction, $1/2$.

(b) interview $\to$ hired $\leftarrow$ referral. The records condition
on hired $= 1$, a collider.

(c) In the applicant pool the two are unrelated. The negative
association among hires was created by the hiring rule: a referred hire
did not need a good interview to get in, and an unreferred hire did.
Nothing about referrals and the quality of candidates follows. The
people who pay are the next referred applicants, held to a higher bar
because of a pattern the company's own rule produced. The records
describe the rule, not the candidates.

(d) With a referral: $q$. Without: $1$. The gap is $1 - q$, so it depends
on $q$, and it is zero only if everyone does well at the interview.
:::

### Exercise 2. The unaware model, with a smaller coaching effect

Leaving a protected characteristic out of a model is often done in the
name of fairness. This exercise computes what it buys, in the lecture's
model with a smaller coaching effect.

Job performance $Y \sim N(0, 1)$, larger is better. A group $A \in
\{0, 1\}$, half the population each, independent of $Y$. A test score
$X = Y + A + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 1)$ independent of
both: group 1 gets one point from coaching, and nothing else. (The
lecture had two points, $\beta_A = 2$; here $\beta_A = 1$.)

(a) Compute $E[X]$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$. The *unaware* model is the regression of $Y$
on $X$: give its prediction $\hat Y$ as a function of $X$, and the
average prediction in each group.

(b) The *full* model uses $X$ and $A$. Within group $a$,
$X - a = Y + \varepsilon$. Give the full model's prediction, the
coefficient on $A$, and the average prediction in each group.

(c) Compute the mean squared error of each model. Which is more
accurate, and which predicts a bigger gap between the groups?

(d) Someone reads the coefficient on $A$ in (b) as the effect of group
membership on job performance. What is wrong with that reading? Which
group does each of the two mistakes, the unaware model's gap and this
reading, fall on?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
The slope of a simple regression is covariance over variance, and the
line passes through the point of means.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
For (c), the mean squared error of the regression of $Y$ on $X$ is
$\operatorname{Var}(Y) - \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)^2/\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $E[X] = E[Y] + E[A] = 1/2$. $\operatorname{Var}(A) = 1/4$, so
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = 1 + 1/4 + 1 = 9/4$. $A$ and $\varepsilon$ are
independent of $Y$, so $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 1$.
Slope $1/(9/4) = 4/9$, and the line passes through the means:
$\hat Y = \tfrac49 (X - \tfrac12)$. In group 0, $E[X] = 0$, average
prediction $-2/9$. In group 1, $E[X] = 1$, average prediction $+2/9$.

(b) Within group $a$, regress $Y$ on $X - a = Y + \varepsilon$: slope
$1/(1 + 1) = 1/2$, so $\hat Y = \tfrac12 (X - A) = \tfrac12 X - \tfrac12 A$.
The coefficient on $A$ is $-1/2$. Average prediction $\tfrac12 E[Y] = 0$
in each group.

(c) Unaware: $\operatorname{Var}(Y) - \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)^2/\operatorname{Var}(X) = 1 - 4/9 = 5/9$.
Full: $1 - 1/2 = 1/2$ in each group. The full model is more accurate,
and it predicts no gap. The unaware model predicts a gap of $4/9$ of a
standard deviation where there is none.

(d) The coefficient is a statement about prediction among people with
the same score: at a given score, group 1 does worse, because part of
its score came from coaching. Changing someone's group would not change
their $Y$ at all. $X$ is a collider between $A$ and $Y$, and
conditioning on it created the association. The comparison of group
means, which does not condition on $X$, gives the right answer, $0$.
The two mistakes fall on different groups. The unaware model's gap
favors the coached group and costs the uncoached one, by $4/9$ of a
standard deviation in the average prediction. The causal
reading of the coefficient says the coached group is worse at the job,
which is false. Neither is a fact about the people; both are facts
about what was done with the data.
:::

### Exercise 3. Inverse probability weighting

$X$ is always recorded and $Y$ is sometimes missing; $C = 1$ when it is
recorded, and $e(X) = P(C = 1 \mid X) > 0$ for every value of $X$.

(a) Show that under MAR, $E\!\left[\dfrac{C\,Y}{e(X)}\right] = E[Y]$.
Say where MAR is used, and where the condition $e(X) > 0$ is used.

(b) In the lecture's income example, $X$ is age (young or old, half
each), the young earn 40 on average and answer with probability 0.8,
the old earn 60 on average and answer with probability 0.4. Compute the
weighted mean and compare it with the mean of the recorded incomes,
46.7.

(c) In practice $e(X)$ is not known. Say in one sentence how you would
estimate it from the data, and what the estimate uses that the
complete-case mean throws away.

(d) The weighted mean assumes that the old people who did not answer
earn what the old people who did answer earn. The complete-case mean
assumes something too: say what. Which assumption would you rather
defend to the people who did not answer, and what would it take to
check either?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
Condition on $X$ first: $E[CY/e(X)] = E\big[E[CY \mid X]/e(X)\big]$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
Under MAR, $C$ and $Y$ are independent given $X$, so
$E[CY \mid X] = E[C \mid X]\,E[Y \mid X]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $E[CY/e(X)] = E\big[E[CY \mid X]/e(X)\big]$ by iterated
expectation, since $e(X)$ is a function of $X$. MAR says $C$ is
independent of $Y$ given $X$, so $E[CY \mid X] = E[C \mid X]\,E[Y \mid X]
= e(X)\,E[Y \mid X]$. Dividing by $e(X)$ needs $e(X) > 0$: a group
nobody answers in cannot be reweighted. What is left is
$E\big[E[Y \mid X]\big] = E[Y]$.

(b) $\tfrac12(0.8)(40)/0.8 + \tfrac12(0.4)(60)/0.4 = 20 + 30 = 50$, the
true mean. The recorded incomes average $46.7$ because the young, who
earn less, answer more often.

(c) Regress the indicator $C$ on $X$ (a logistic regression, or the
share answering at each value of $X$), and use the fitted probabilities
as $e(X)$. The estimate uses the rows where $Y$ is missing: their $X$
is recorded, and it is what tells you who did not answer.

(d) The complete-case mean assumes that the people who did not answer
earn what the people who did answer earn, whatever their age: MCAR. The
recorded data already contradict it, since response differs by age.
The weights assume MAR given age, which the recorded data can neither
confirm nor refute: within an age group, nothing recorded says whether
the silent earn more or less than the rest. Checking either would mean
asking some of the people who did not answer, that is, collecting what
was not collected. The weights do not escape the assumption; they
write it down. The complete-case mean rests on an assumption too, and
nobody wrote it down. A written assumption can be challenged by the
people it is about, and an unwritten one cannot.
:::

## In class

### Discussion 1: who is missing from the data you brought

Use the dataset or study you brought, where some people who should be
in it are not. If you did not bring one, choose: a customer
satisfaction survey; a hospital's records of patient outcomes; a
university's record of its graduates' salaries; the crimes recorded by
the police; a dating app's record of which matches led to a date.

1. Who is missing, and which way does their absence push the result?
   Who is better off for that?
2. Relative to what the dataset records about people, is the
   missingness closer to completely at random, at random, or not at
   random? What would the dataset have to record to make it "at
   random"?
3. Name one dataset that should exist and does not. Who would have had
   to collect it, and why have they not?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Some examples" collapse="true"}
- A satisfaction survey: the people who left are not there to be
  asked, and the furious and the delighted answer more than the
  middle. Which direction depends on the mix; the spread is too wide
  and the mean is pulled toward whichever end answers more. The firm
  that reports the score is better off whenever the people who left
  were the unhappy ones. Nothing recorded about the people who left
  makes it MAR; a record of who was invited, with what they had bought,
  would help.
- Graduates' salaries: people who did not find work, or did not want
  to say, do not answer, so the mean is too high, and the university
  that prints it in its prospectus is better off. MNAR, since the
  salary itself drives the answer. Recording employment status for
  everyone, from a separate source, would move it toward MAR.
- Recorded crime: crimes nobody reported and places nobody patrolled.
  The direction depends on the crime; the record is too high where the
  police look, and the people who live there pay for it in the next
  round of patrols.
- A dataset that should exist: the lecture's own case, how often
  detained defendants would have returned to court; or deaths in
  custody, counted by the institution that held the person; or the
  wages of people paid in cash. The institution that would have to
  collect it is often the one the data would judge.
:::

### Problem 1. Why is it missing, and which way?

(a) For each setting, say whether the missing values are MCAR, MAR or
MNAR, and whether the mean of the recorded values is too high, too
low, or neither, compared with the mean for everyone. Say which clause
of the setting your answer depends on, and who is worse off if the
recorded mean is taken at face value.

  - A fitness watch records resting heart rate only on nights it is
    worn. People take it off on nights they feel unwell, and nothing
    else about them is recorded.
  - Exam marks are missing for students whose exam scripts were lost
    in the post; the post lost one sack at random.
  - A survey asks about weekly hours worked, and the overall mean will
    set one staffing standard for both regions. Response is lower in
    one region than another, the region is recorded, and within each
    region whether someone responds is unrelated to their hours.

(b) A company surveys its staff about pay. Half are junior, with mean
salary 30 (thousands), and half are senior, with mean salary 70.
Juniors respond with probability 0.9 and seniors with probability 0.3.
Within each grade, whether someone responds is unrelated to their
salary. What is the true mean salary? What is the mean among
respondents? Check your answer with
$E[Y \mid C = 1] - E[Y] = \operatorname{Cov}(Y, C)/P(C = 1)$.

(c) Weight each respondent by one over their grade's response
probability. Show that the weighted mean recovers the true mean. (For
100 staff: how many respondents are in each grade, and what weight does
each get?)

(d) Now suppose that within each grade the better-paid staff respond
less often. Is the weighted mean from (c) still right? Which way is it
wrong, and what would fix it? Who would have to agree to the fix?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (b): $E[YC]$ is the average over everyone of salary times the
response indicator, so sum salary times response probability over the
two grades, each with weight $1/2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
For (c): of 100 staff, 50 are junior and 45 of them respond.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) The watch: MNAR. Whether a night is recorded depends on feeling
unwell, which is related to heart rate and is not recorded; the clause
"nothing else about them is recorded" is what rules out MAR. Recorded
nights are healthier nights, so the mean resting heart rate is too
low, and the wearer is worse off: the nights a doctor would want to
see are the ones not there. Lost scripts: MCAR, because the sack was
lost at random; without that clause (if the post lost the sack from
one school) it need not be. The mean is unbiased, just based on fewer
students; nobody is misled by it, though the students whose scripts
were lost have a different problem. Hours by region: MAR given region,
and the clause "within each region ... unrelated to their hours" is
doing the work. The overall mean is biased toward the region that
responds more, in the direction of that region's mean, so the standard
is set closer to the hours of the region that answered more, and the
other region works to a number that is mostly not its own.

(b) True mean $\tfrac12(30) + \tfrac12(70) = 50$.
$P(C = 1) = \tfrac12(0.9) + \tfrac12(0.3) = 0.6$.
$E[YC] = \tfrac12(0.9)(30) + \tfrac12(0.3)(70) = 13.5 + 10.5 = 24$, so
the respondents' mean is $24/0.6 = 40$, too low by 10. Check:
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y, C) = 24 - 50 \times 0.6 = -6$, and $-6/0.6 = -10$.

(c) Of 100 staff, 45 juniors and 15 seniors respond. Juniors get weight
$1/0.9$, seniors $1/0.3$. Weighted mean
$(45 \times 30/0.9 + 15 \times 70/0.3)/100 = (1500 + 3500)/100 = 50$.
In general $E[CY/e(X)] = E[Y]$ when response depends only on the
recorded grade $X$, with $e(X) = P(C = 1 \mid X)$ (exercise 3).

(d) No. Missingness now depends on salary within grade, which is MNAR.
The weights correct for the difference between grades but not within
them: within each grade the respondents are the lower paid, so the
weighted mean is still too low. Nothing computed from the recorded
salaries fixes it; what would is a recorded variable that explains who
answers within a grade (a pay band from the payroll, say), or an
assumption about the non-respondents that someone is prepared to
defend. The payroll fix uses data the staff gave for another purpose,
so the staff, or whoever speaks for them, would have to agree to it.
The assumption fix needs no one's agreement, which is why it has to be
written down and defended rather than made in private.
:::

### Discussion 2: why leave out $A$?

In the lecture's test-score example, the model that leaves the group
$A$ out is less accurate in both groups and predicts a gap between
groups whose $Y$ has the same distribution.

1. Write the strongest argument for leaving $A$ out, and the strongest
   argument against. Then say which causal graph each argument
   assumes.
2. Now $A$ is not a protected characteristic but a column that was
   recorded for half the applicants. Would you drop the column, drop
   the rows that lack it, or fill it in? Who would you have to justify
   the choice to, and could you?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Some directions" collapse="true"}
1. For leaving it out: a model that uses $A$ gives two people with the
   same score different predictions because of their group, which is
   the shape of direct discrimination (Equality Act 2010, section 13),
   and if $A$ had shaped the recorded outcome itself, a model using $A$
   would learn and repeat that; this assumes a graph with an arrow from
   $A$ into $Y$ or into how $Y$ was measured. Against: in the lecture's
   graph $A$ affects the score and not the outcome, so leaving it out
   makes the model read coaching as ability, less accurate for
   everyone and worse for the group without coaching; a rule applied
   to all that disadvantages one group is the shape of indirect
   discrimination (section 19), unless justified. Neither argument
   works in the other's graph, and the data do not say which graph
   holds.
2. The lecture's table: dropping the column loses accuracy and creates
   the gap for everyone; dropping the rows keeps a correct model for
   the people who have $A$ and no prediction for the rest; filling in
   recovers the fit but, for a row without $A$, predicts from $X$ alone
   and keeps the gap. The question is who the model is for. The
   justification goes to whoever is scored by it, and to whoever asks
   later why a column is absent; "the software dropped it" is not an
   answer anyone can defend, and the point of the exercise is that it
   is the most common one.
:::

### Coding: filling in, four ways

One laptop between two. You need `ggplot2`, `dplyr` and `mice`
(`install.packages("mice")` once). $Y$ depends on $X$, and we remove
values of $Y$ in three ways, then estimate the mean of $Y$ four ways.

```{r filling_starter, eval=FALSE}
library(mice)
n <- 2000
X <- rnorm(n)
Y <- 1 + X + rnorm(n)                       # the truth: E[Y] = 1, slope 1
logistic <- function(v) 1 / (1 + exp(-v))
C_mcar <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5) == 1            # recorded with probability 1/2, whoever you are
C_mar  <- rbinom(n, 1, logistic(-1.5 * X)) == 1        # recorded less often when X is high
C_mnar <- rbinom(n, 1, logistic(-1.5 * (Y - 1))) == 1  # recorded less often when Y is high
c(mean(C_mcar), mean(C_mar), mean(C_mnar))

estimate <- function(C) {
  d <- data.frame(X = X, Y = ifelse(C, Y, NA))            # Y is NA where it is missing
  cc <- c(mean(d$Y, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$Y, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(C)))
  mean_imp <- ifelse(C, Y, mean(Y[C]))                     # fill the holes with the recorded mean
  mi <- c(mean(mean_imp), sd(mean_imp) / sqrt(n))
  reg_imp <- # ...                                         # fill the holes with the prediction from X
  ri <- c(mean(reg_imp), sd(reg_imp) / sqrt(n))
  imp <- mice(d, m = 20, method = "norm", printFlag = FALSE)   # 20 completions
  pooled <- summary(pool(with(imp, lm(Y ~ 1))))                # the mean of Y in each, pooled
  mult <- c(pooled$estimate, pooled$std.error)
  out <- rbind(`complete cases` = cc, `mean imputation` = mi,
               `regression imputation` = ri, `multiple imputation` = mult)
  colnames(out) <- c("estimate", "se")
  out
}
```

1. Run the first block. Each indicator keeps about half the rows.
   Before you estimate anything, write down for each of the three
   indicators whether you expect the complete-case mean to be too
   high, too low, or right, and why.
2. Complete the regression-imputation line: fit `lm(Y ~ X, data = d)`
   on the rows that have $Y$ (which is what `lm()` does with `NA`) and
   fill each hole with its prediction. Then run `estimate()` on each
   indicator and put the three tables side by side. The truth is $1$;
   the standard error of the mean of all $n$ values of $Y$ would be
   about $\sqrt{2/n} = 0.032$, and of half of them about $0.045$.
3. Read the tables by row. Which methods are biased under which
   mechanism? Which standard errors are too small, and what makes them
   too small? What does multiple imputation fix that regression
   imputation does not, and what does it not fix?
4. Look inside `mice`. For the MAR data, `imp <- mice(d, m = 20,
   method = "norm", printFlag = FALSE)`; then `head(imp$imp$Y[, 1:4])`
   shows the first four completions' values for the first few missing
   rows, and `pool(with(imp, lm(Y ~ 1)))$pooled` shows `ubar` (the
   average within-completion variance), `b` (the variance of the 20
   estimates) and `t` (the total). Check that
   $t = \bar u + (1 + 1/m)\,b$. Which of the three is what a single
   fill-in throws away?
5. Every row of the MNAR column is wrong, multiple imputation included,
   because every method assumed that the missing $Y$ are like the
   recorded $Y$ with the same $X$. An imputation model is an assumption
   about people who are not in the data. A statistics office imputes
   missing incomes in a survey that is used to set benefit levels. Who
   should choose the model, what should be published about it, and who
   would read it?
6. At home: real data. R's `airquality` (New York, May to September
   1973) has 37 missing ozone readings out of 153. Tabulate the share
   missing by month. Estimate the mean ozone level by complete cases,
   mean imputation, and multiple imputation using `Temp`, `Wind` and
   `Month`. What does the multiple imputation assume about the days
   with missing ozone that no check on the data can confirm?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For step 2: `reg_imp <- ifelse(C, Y, predict(lm(Y ~ X, data = d), newdata = d))`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
For step 3: a standard error of the mean has the spread of the values
on top and $\sqrt{n}$ underneath. Ask what each fill-in does to each.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r filling_solution}
n <- 2000
X <- rnorm(n)
Y <- 1 + X + rnorm(n)
logistic <- function(v) 1 / (1 + exp(-v))
C_mcar <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5) == 1
C_mar  <- rbinom(n, 1, logistic(-1.5 * X)) == 1
C_mnar <- rbinom(n, 1, logistic(-1.5 * (Y - 1))) == 1
estimate <- function(C) {
  d <- data.frame(X = X, Y = ifelse(C, Y, NA))
  cc <- c(mean(d$Y, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$Y, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(C)))
  mean_imp <- ifelse(C, Y, mean(Y[C]))
  mi <- c(mean(mean_imp), sd(mean_imp) / sqrt(n))
  reg_imp <- ifelse(C, Y, predict(lm(Y ~ X, data = d), newdata = d))
  ri <- c(mean(reg_imp), sd(reg_imp) / sqrt(n))
  imp <- mice(d, m = 20, method = "norm", printFlag = FALSE)
  pooled <- summary(pool(with(imp, lm(Y ~ 1))))
  mult <- c(pooled$estimate, pooled$std.error)
  out <- rbind(`complete cases` = cc, `mean imputation` = mi,
               `regression imputation` = ri, `multiple imputation` = mult)
  colnames(out) <- c("estimate", "se")
  out
}
res <- list(MCAR = estimate(C_mcar), MAR = estimate(C_mar), MNAR = estimate(C_mnar))
side_by_side <- do.call(cbind, lapply(names(res), function(k) {
  m <- res[[k]]; colnames(m) <- paste(k, colnames(m)); m }))
round(side_by_side, 3)                                        # steps 2 and 3
mean(Y)                                                       # this sample's full mean

d <- data.frame(X = X, Y = ifelse(C_mar, Y, NA))              # step 4
imp <- mice(d, m = 20, method = "norm", printFlag = FALSE)
head(imp$imp$Y[, 1:4], 3)
pool(with(imp, lm(Y ~ 1)))$pooled[, c("estimate", "ubar", "b", "t", "m")]
```

1. MCAR: right, with more variance. MAR: too low, because the rows
   with high $X$, which have high $Y$, go missing more often. MNAR:
   too low, because the high $Y$ themselves go missing.
2. and 3. Read across. Under MCAR every estimate is right; mean
   imputation and regression imputation report standard errors about
   half the right size, because they count $n$ values where there were
   $n/2$ and the filled-in values have less spread than real ones.
   Under MAR the complete-case mean and mean imputation are far too
   low (mean imputation puts the complete-case mean into every hole, so
   it cannot move the mean); regression imputation gets the mean right,
   because the regression of $Y$ on $X$ is correct and $X$ is recorded
   for everyone, but its standard error is still too small; multiple
   imputation gets the mean right and a standard error close to what
   half the data deserve. Under MNAR every method is wrong, multiple
   imputation included: all four use the recorded $X$ to say what the
   missing $Y$ are like, and here the missingness depends on $Y$
   itself, which no recorded variable explains. Multiple imputation
   fixes the standard error, not the assumption.
4. The four columns differ row by row: each completion is a draw, not
   a prediction. `b` is the variance of the 20 estimates across
   completions, and it is what a single fill-in throws away;
   `t = ubar + (1 + 1/20) b`.
5. Directions, not an answer. The model decides what the people who
   did not answer are taken to earn, and the benefit level follows, so
   the choice is about them and is made without them. Whoever chooses
   should be able to say which recorded variables the imputation uses,
   which way the estimate would move if the silent earn less than the
   model says (the MNAR column), and how much. That is what should be
   published, in a form the people whose benefits depend on it, and
   those who speak for them, can read; the usual answer, a line in a
   technical appendix nobody opens, is a choice made in private about
   people who were not asked. Note what the table showed: none of the
   four methods can tell you from the data which column you are in.
6. In June 70% of ozone readings are missing, in September 3%, so the
   data are not MCAR. Mean imputation's standard error is the smallest
   and is wrong, for the reason in step 3. The multiple imputation
   assumes that, given temperature, wind and month, the missing days'
   ozone is like the recorded days' ozone: MAR given those variables.
   If the instrument failed on days of unusual ozone, that is false,
   and no check on the recorded data can show it.
:::

### Problem 2. Selection on a collider, with numbers

A university admits by exam grade. Grades run from 1 to 10, each
equally likely among applicants. Half the applicants come from a feeder
school, independently of their grade. The pass mark is 7, and 5 for
applicants from a feeder school. The university's records cover
admitted students only.

(a) Among admitted students, what is the mean grade of those from a
feeder school, and of those not from one?

(b) Draw the causal graph with nodes grade, feeder school and admitted,
and mark what the records condition on.

(c) An analyst concludes from the records that feeder schools produce
weaker students, and the university considers withdrawing the lower
pass mark. What is wrong, and who would pay for the mistake?

(d) Write down an admission rule under which, among the admitted,
feeder-school students have the *higher* mean grade. What does this
say about what the graph alone tells you, and about what the records
are a record of?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
Among the admitted, which grades can a feeder-school student have, and
which can a student from elsewhere have?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
For (d), make the feeder school's bar the higher one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) Admitted students not from a feeder school have grades 7 to 10,
mean $8.5$. Admitted students from a feeder school have grades 5 to 10,
mean $7.5$. The band 5 to 6 holds feeder-school students only.

(b) grade $\to$ admitted $\leftarrow$ feeder school. The records
condition on admitted $= 1$, a collider.

(c) Among applicants, grade and school are unrelated: the mean grade is
$5.5$ in both groups. The difference among the admitted was created by
the rule, which let feeder-school applicants in on lower grades.
Nothing about what feeder schools do to their students follows.
"Produce" is a causal claim, and the records cannot support it. The
mistake would fall on the next feeder-school applicants, who would
lose the lower pass mark on the strength of a pattern that the lower
pass mark itself produced.

(d) A pass mark of 9 for feeder-school applicants and 7 for everyone
else: means $9.5$ and $8.5$, the feeder-school students higher. The
graph says that conditioning on the collider creates an association;
the rule says which way. Without the rule, "depends on both" does not
fix the sign (the lecture's notes, after the noisy collider). The
association among the admitted is a record of the university's rule,
a decision someone made and could change, and not of the students.
:::

### Discussion 3: a label that exists only where a decision allowed it

A bank wants to know whether a new credit-scoring model would make
better lending decisions than its current one. It evaluates the new
model on its past applicants. It only knows whether an applicant repaid
if it approved them.

1. Who is missing from the evaluation, and by what mechanism? Which
   way are the new model's measured error rates likely to be wrong?
2. Who benefits from the problem going unnoticed?
3. The honest fix is to approve some applicants the current model
   rejects, chosen at random, and record what happens. Who pays for
   that, and is it justified?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Some directions" collapse="true"}
1. The applicants the old model rejected: their repayment is not
   observed. If the old model rejected on things the new model also
   uses, the rejected are the ones expected to default, so the
   approved pool is safer than the applicant pool, and among them
   default is rare: MNAR by the decision the data are meant to evaluate
   (the lecture's selective labels). The new model's measured default
   rate among the people it would approve is too low, and its errors on
   people the old model rejected are invisible. If the old model
   rejected on things the new model does not use, the direction is not
   determined without more.
2. Whoever sells the new model, which looks better than it is; the
   bank, in the short run, which gets a number it can report; and
   nobody who was rejected, since their outcomes are the ones not
   counted. Lakkaraju and colleagues' remedy, for judges, used the fact
   that decision-makers differ in leniency and cases are assigned to
   them at random; a bank with one policy has no lenient judge to
   compare with, which is why question 3's fix is the one that does
   not rest on an assumption about the people rejected.
3. The bank pays, in the defaults among the randomly approved, and so
   do the randomly approved who default, since a loan one cannot repay
   is not a gift. The people who gain are the rejected applicants who
   would have repaid, who are exactly the people the current records
   cannot see, and every future applicant scored by a model whose
   errors were measured on everyone. Whether that is justified is a
   choice, and the two sides are not symmetric: the cost of the fix is
   visible and falls on the bank, the cost of not fixing it is
   invisible and falls on the people wrongly rejected. "We evaluate on
   the data we have" sounds neutral and is a decision in favor of the
   visible cost.
:::

## For next time

Bring one rule or score that sorts people into two groups: admit or
reject, flag or clear, treat or not. Write down the two ways it can be
wrong, and who pays for each. One sentence each.
